name: Castoreum

lead: Castoreum is a yellowish secretion from the castor sacs of beavers, which the animals use to scent-mark territory. Perfumers dry the sacs, age them and tincture them in alcohol to make a resinoid prized for a leather-like note, so it is part of how some colognes and perfumes smell warm, smoky and distinctive.

Its appearance payoff is indirect: it shapes the fragrance a person wears, not their skin or features. Published research covers its safety as a flavour and fragrance ingredient and the chemistry of the beaver secretion, not any effect on attractiveness.

paras: Wearers meet castoreum as one ingredient in finished fragrances, typically classic leather or oriental scents, rather than as a product used alone. Perfumery guides describe it as blended with other materials instead of worn neat.

A 2007 safety review found castoreum extract nontoxic in animal tests, not a skin irritant and not a sensitizer in human tests, and regulators list it as generally recognized as safe as a food flavour. It is an animal-derived ingredient, which matters to people who avoid such products.

angle.text: Castoreum is an ingredient in perfumes that people wear to smell distinctive. It affects presentation through scent, not through any change to skin, hair or body.

lead: Castoreum is the yellowish exudate stored in the castor sacs of mature beavers. Beavers mix it with urine to mark territory, and it contains dozens of identified compounds, including phenols with pheromonal activity.[1][2][3] In perfumery the word usually means a resinoid made by drying and aging the sacs and extracting them in alcohol.[1]

For looks, castoreum matters through scent: it contributes a leather-like, animalic warmth to blended fragrances, and classic perfumes such as Chanel's Antaeus and Shalimar are cited as examples.[1] Many modern fragrances rely on synthetic accords instead, and ordinary wearers meet castoreum, if at all, as a name in a fragrance note list.
Published research on castoreum concerns beaver chemical ecology and food-ingredient safety. No human study has examined whether wearing it changes how attractive a person is perceived to be.

Rare in food; niche in perfumery

paras: Castoreum comes from the castor sacs, which both male and female beavers have and which are not true glands at the cellular level. Beavers deposit it on scent mounds, and field analyses in Norway found castoreum compounds in all 96 scent marks collected on snow.[2][3]

Chemists have characterized its large phenolic fraction, which accounts for much of its distinctive odour, and found that mixtures of synthetic compounds draw weaker responses from beavers than natural castoreum.[4][5]

Perfumers use a resinoid from dried castor sacs that are aged for two or more years, valued mainly for a leather-like note that is blended with other ingredients.[1] It has also been a flavouring: castoreum extract has been added to food for at least 80 years, though today's industry use is a very small amount compared with vanillin.[6][1]

In the United States the FDA and the flavor manufacturers' association classify castoreum extract as generally recognized as safe, and a 1965 FEMA programme listed castoreum extract and castoreum liquid.[6][1]

A 2007 review in the International Journal of Toxicology reported that castoreum extract was nontoxic by oral and dermal routes in animals, not irritating or phototoxic, and not a skin sensitizer in human subject tests. It noted no reports of human adverse reactions despite long use.[6]

No studies found on castoreum and attractiveness or appearance. Safety testing of the extract is described under Safety, and a small 2024 study used castoreum as a control odour in children's ratings of body-odour smells.[6][7]
